etymology: Simon Peter, chief of the Twelve; the Lord named him Cephas (Aramaic) / Petros (Greek), “a stone.”
biblical_def: Peter the apostle, Simon son of Jonas, was the fisherman of Galilee whom the Lord called, renamed Cephas (a stone), and made the foremost spokesman of the Twelve. His life is a portrait of grace at work in a bold, impulsive, faltering, and finally faithful man. He made the great confession—Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God—which the Lord said the Father had revealed to him. He walked on the water and sank; he protested he would never deny his Lord and then denied Him thrice; yet the Lord had prayed for him that his faith should not fail, and bade him, when converted, to strengthen his brethren. Restored by the risen Christ and filled with the Spirit at Pentecost, he stood up with the eleven and preached the sermon by which three thousand were converted, opening the door of faith to Jew and, at Cornelius’s house, to Gentile. He wrote two epistles and, by tradition, was martyred at Rome. The dictionary honors Peter as the bold confessor and restored sinner, the Spirit-filled preacher of Pentecost; and it refuses the Roman claim built upon him—that he was the first pope, supreme over the apostles, his supposed successors infallible. Peter himself wrote not as a prince but as a fellow-elder, pointing the flock not to himself but to the Chief Shepherd.
webster_summary: Simon Peter, chief spokesman of the Twelve; the bold confessor, restored denier, and Pentecost preacher—honored as apostle, not as the first pope, for he called himself a fellow-elder.

corruption_summary: Rome makes Peter the first pope, supreme over the apostles with infallible successors; Scripture shows him a fellow-apostle and self-named fellow-elder, rebuked by Paul and pointing the flock to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the Roman edifice built upon Peter: that the Lord’s word, thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, made him the first pope, monarch over the apostles and the whole church, with a line of infallible successors at Rome. But the rock on which the church is built is the confession Peter had just made, Christ the Son of the living God—and Christ Himself is the chief corner stone, the apostles and prophets together the foundation. Peter exercised no monarchy: he was sent by the apostles, rebuked to his face by Paul, and called himself merely a fellow-elder and a witness, pointing not to himself but to the Chief Shepherd.

The principle to recover is Peter as the bold confessor and restored sinner, a fellow-apostle and not a prince. His life magnifies grace: the man who sank in the water, who denied his Lord with oaths, was prayed for that his faith should not fail, restored by the risen Christ, and made the Pentecost preacher of the gospel he had once denied. He wrote as a fellow-elder, exhorting shepherds to feed the flock willingly and not as lords; and his confidence and the church’s rest not on his throne but on the Christ he confessed. The keys he received were the keys of the gospel, given to the whole church, not a crown set upon one man’s head.

etymology: One of the twelve apostles, of Bethsaida; Greek Philippos, “lover of horses”; to be distinguished from Philip the evangelist of Acts.
biblical_def: Philip the apostle was one of the Twelve, a man of Bethsaida in Galilee, the same town as Peter and Andrew, and he is to be distinguished from Philip the evangelist and deacon of the book of Acts. The Gospel of John gives us our clearest glimpses of him. Called by the Lord with the simple word Follow me, Philip at once sought his friend Nathanael: We have found him, of whom Moses in the law and the prophets did write, Jesus of Nazareth—and when Nathanael doubted, Philip answered with the best of all invitations, Come and see. It was to Philip the Lord tested the question of feeding the five thousand; and when certain Greeks came up to the feast desiring to see Jesus, they came to Philip. In the upper room Philip made the request that drew out one of the Lord’s greatest sayings: Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us—to which Jesus answered, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father. The dictionary reads Philip the apostle as the disciple who found the Lord and at once brought another, and whose honest, half-understanding question opened to the church the truth that to see Christ is to see the Father—a reminder that the apostles were plain men brought along slowly into great light, and that the answer to every seeker remains, Come and see.
webster_summary: One of the Twelve, of Bethsaida; who brought Nathanael with “Come and see,” and whose request “shew us the Father” drew out the Lord’s word that to see Him is to see the Father.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though Philip the apostle is often confused with Philip the evangelist; the chief truth is his witness that to see Christ is to see the Father.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to clarify is the common confusion of the two Philips of the New Testament. Philip the apostle was one of the Twelve, called early in John’s Gospel; Philip the evangelist was one of the seven chosen to serve tables in Acts 6, who later preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch. They are two men, and the careful reader keeps them distinct. Beyond this, no great corruption attends the apostle; the chief thing is rather to receive the truth his questions drew out and not to pass him by as a minor figure.

The principle to recover is the great truth Philip’s request occasioned: that to see Christ is to see the Father. When Philip said, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us, the Lord answered, He that hath seen me hath seen the Father—for the Son is the express image of the Father’s person, and in Him the invisible God is made known. Philip’s honest, half-understanding request opened to the church one of the clearest words of Christ’s deity and His revelation of the Father. And his first act after being found—to find Nathanael and say, Come and see—remains the model of the disciple who, having found the Lord, brings another to Him.

etymology: A believer at Rome greeted by Paul (Romans 16:15); Greek Philologos, “lover of the word” or “fond of learning.”
biblical_def: Philologus was a believer in the church at Rome, named among the long list of saints Paul greets at the close of his epistle to the Romans: Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them. Nothing more is known of him—no deed recorded, no office named, no further word—and herein lies his quiet importance. Philologus is one of the obscure saints of Scripture, known to us by name only because the Spirit moved Paul to greet him; yet he was known fully to God, his name written, the dictionary trusts, in the Lamb’s book of life. The Scripture honors such hidden saints: a book of remembrance was written before the LORD for them that feared Him and thought upon His name; the Lord bade His disciples rejoice that their names are written in heaven; Paul speaks of his fellowlabourers whose names are in the book of life. The dictionary reads Philologus as a representative of the countless unsung believers—the faithful obscure, who hold no office and leave no monument, yet are loved by Christ, greeted by name, and remembered before God. His one-word mention is a comfort to every hidden saint: that no believer is anonymous to God, that the humblest member of the church is named and known and dear to the Lord, and that the book of remembrance holds the names the world forgets.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age prizes only the famous and forgets the obscure; Scripture honors the hidden saint, named and loved by God though the world knows him not.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the age’s idolatry of fame, which measures worth by visibility and forgets entirely the obscure—and which has crept into the church, where celebrity pastors and platformed influencers are honored while the faithful unknown are overlooked. But the Scripture reverses the world’s scale. It pauses to name a Philologus of whom nothing else is recorded, for he was dear to Christ and to the church; and it teaches that a book of remembrance is written before the LORD for them that fear Him, and that the names to rejoice over are those written in heaven—not the names trending on the earth.

The principle to recover is the honor God gives the hidden saint. Philologus held no office we know, did no deed Scripture records, left no monument; yet he is named, because he was known and loved by God. The Lord bids His people rejoice not in visible success but that their names are written in heaven; Paul remembers fellowlabourers whose names are in the book of life. This is a deep comfort to every obscure believer who serves unseen, suffers unnoticed, and will leave no earthly memorial: no saint is anonymous to God. The humblest member of Christ’s body is named, known, and dear to Him, and the book of remembrance holds the names the world forgets.

etymology: The church founded by Paul in the Greek city of Corinth, recipient of his two canonical epistles to the Corinthians.
biblical_def: The Corinthian church was the congregation Paul founded in the wealthy, immoral, and cosmopolitan Greek city of Corinth, and it stands in Scripture as the great case study of a gifted but carnal church—rich in grace yet riddled with sin, the recipient of his two searching epistles. The church was truly the church of God, sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, enriched in all utterance and knowledge, coming behind in no gift. Yet it was torn by divisions—I am of Paul, I of Apollos—and Paul had to call them carnal, walking as mere men; it tolerated gross immorality, dragged brother against brother before pagan courts, abused the Lord’s Supper, misused spiritual gifts in disorder, and harbored some who denied the resurrection. To this church Paul wrote the soaring chapter on love and the great chapter on the resurrection, correcting its errors and recalling it to order, holiness, and the supremacy of love. And he reminded them what grace had done: such were some of you—fornicators, idolaters, drunkards—but ye are washed, ye are sanctified, ye are justified. The dictionary reads the Corinthian church as the abiding mirror of a gifted, worldly, struggling congregation: a true church marred by carnality, called back by apostolic correction to unity, purity, and love—a warning that gifts are no measure of maturity, and a comfort that grace can sanctify even a Corinth.

corruption_summary: Corinth’s abundance of gifts amid its carnality warns against measuring spiritual maturity by gifting; the church was called back to holiness, order, and love.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to draw, against a common modern error, is that spiritual gifts are no measure of spiritual maturity. Corinth came behind in no gift—tongues, prophecy, knowledge, utterance abounded—and yet Paul called them carnal, babes in Christ, walking as mere men. The age that prizes spectacular gifting, dramatic experience, and crowded auditoriums as the proof of God’s blessing should sit long with Corinth, where every gift flourished and the love was thin, the unity broken, and the immorality tolerated. Gifts adorn a church; they do not sanctify it.

The principle to recover is the call back to holiness, order, and love. To this gifted and carnal church Paul wrote not to flatter its gifts but to correct its sins—to heal its divisions, purge its immorality, order its worship, and crown all with the love without which the greatest gifts are nothing. He recalled them to what grace had made them: washed, sanctified, justified, though such things some of them had been. The Corinthian church stands as both warning and comfort: a warning that gifting is not godliness, and a comfort that the grace which could sanctify a Corinth can sanctify any struggling church that submits to the Word and presses on to love.

etymology: One of the seven churches of Asia addressed in Revelation 2–3; Sardis, the ancient capital of Lydia.
biblical_def: The church of Sardis was one of the seven churches of Asia to which the risen Christ sent letters through John in the Revelation, and it received the most solemn warning of all—the church with a reputation for life that was, in truth, dead. To Sardis the Lord said, I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead. Outwardly the church flourished, esteemed by men, with a name for vitality; inwardly it was a corpse, its works not found perfect before God, its spiritual life all but extinguished. The Lord’s charge was urgent: be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die; remember how thou hast received and heard, and hold fast, and repent. If thou shalt not watch, I will come on thee as a thief. Yet even in dead Sardis there was a remnant: thou hast a few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments, and they shall walk with me in white, for they are worthy. The dictionary reads the church of Sardis as the abiding warning against dead orthodoxy and reputation without reality—the church that men praise and God indicts, alive in name and dead in fact—and as a call to watchfulness, repentance, and the strengthening of what remains; with the comfort that even in the deadest church God preserves His undefiled few, who shall walk with Christ in white.

corruption_summary: Sardis warns against the dead orthodoxy and reputation-without-reality that men praise and God indicts; the call is to watch, repent, and strengthen what remains.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption Sardis embodies is dead orthodoxy—a church with a name for life but no life, esteemed by men yet a corpse before God. It is a peril of sound churches especially: a congregation may keep the right doctrine, the old forms, the respected name, and the busy programs, while the Spirit has withdrawn and the works are found imperfect before God—outwardly alive, inwardly dead. The age that measures a church by its reputation, its size, or its heritage may praise a Sardis that God indicts; and the danger is the more deadly because it wears the appearance of health.

The principle to recover is watchfulness, repentance, and the strengthening of what remains. The risen Christ does not abandon dead Sardis but commands it to wake: be watchful, strengthen the things that remain and are ready to die, remember what you received, hold fast, and repent—or He will come as a thief. And He gives the comfort that even in the deadest church He preserves a faithful remnant: a few names that have not defiled their garments, who shall walk with Him in white. The lesson for every church is to seek not a name for life but life itself, in the reality of the Spirit’s presence and the fruit of true godliness, lest it be alive in name and dead in fact.

etymology: The churches Paul founded in Macedonia—Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea—in response to the Macedonian call.
biblical_def: The Macedonian churches were the congregations Paul planted in the northern Greek province of Macedonia—chiefly Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea—and they are remembered in Scripture for their faith, their generosity, and their steadfastness under affliction. Their founding came by a heavenly summons: a vision appeared to Paul in the night of a man of Macedonia, praying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us—and so the gospel first crossed into Europe. At Philippi a church was born of Lydia and the jailer; at Thessalonica believers turned from idols to serve the living God and became ensamples to all that believe in Macedonia and Achaia, their faith sounding out everywhere; at Berea the hearers were more noble, receiving the word with all readiness and searching the Scriptures daily. These churches, though poor and persecuted, abounded in liberality, pressing upon Paul their gift for the poor saints, and the Philippians alone shared with him in his need again and again. The dictionary reads the Macedonian churches as a model of gospel grace under hardship: born of a heavenly call, marked by a faith that sounded abroad, a generosity that gave out of deep poverty, and a steadfastness under persecution—a standing example that the richest churches in grace are often the poorest in goods, and that affliction and liberality may flourish together where the gospel has truly taken root.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to weigh, against the worldly measure of a church’s success, is that the Macedonian churches were poor and persecuted yet rich in grace. The modern mind—and much of the modern church—reckons prosperity, size, and ease the marks of God’s blessing, and would have counted these afflicted, impoverished congregations as struggling failures. But Scripture holds them up as ensamples to all that believe: their faith sounded out everywhere, their generosity abounded out of deep poverty, and their steadfastness shone under persecution. The richest churches in grace were among the poorest in goods.

The principle to recover is that gospel grace flourishes under hardship. The Macedonian churches were born of a heavenly call—Come over and help us—and grew amid affliction into models of faith, liberality, and endurance: Thessalonica an ensample whose faith rang out, Berea noble in searching the Scriptures daily, Philippi sharing in Paul’s need from the first day. Their abounding joy and deep poverty overflowed in liberality. They teach the church of every age that affliction and generosity may flourish together, that the measure of a church is grace and not goods, and that where the gospel truly takes root, it bears the richest fruit in the hardest soil.

etymology: From the poor widow who cast two mites into the temple treasury (Mark 12; Luke 21); a mite was the smallest coin.
biblical_def: The widow’s mite is the offering of the poor widow whom the Lord watched cast two mites—the smallest of coins, together making a farthing—into the temple treasury, and whom He declared to have given more than all the rich. Sitting over against the treasury, Jesus beheld how the people cast in their money, and many that were rich cast in much; and there came a certain poor widow who threw in two mites. Calling His disciples, He said, Verily I say unto you, that this poor widow hath cast more in than all they which have cast into the treasury; for all they did cast in of their abundance, but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living. The Lord’s reckoning overturns the world’s: He measures the gift not by its amount but by the cost to the giver and the love behind it; the rich gave out of their surplus and kept their security, but the widow gave her whole living and cast herself wholly on God. The dictionary reads the widow’s mite as the Lord’s own standard of giving: that God weighs the heart and the sacrifice, not the sum; that the smallest gift given in love and faith, at real cost, is more in His sight than great gifts given easily; and that the poorest saint, giving her all, may give more than the rich, for she gives herself.
webster_summary: The poor widow’s two small coins, which the Lord declared more than all the rich gave; God weighs the gift by the cost to the giver and the love behind it, not by the sum.

corruption_summary: The world measures giving by the sum, honoring the large donor; the Lord measures by the cost to the giver and the love behind it, counting the widow’s mite more than the rich man’s abundance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption the account rebukes is the world’s—and too often the church’s—measuring of giving by the sum, honoring the large donor and overlooking the poor. The rich who cast in much were doubtless esteemed; the widow with her two mites went unnoticed by all but Christ. The age that names buildings after big givers and weighs generosity in dollars has forgotten the Lord’s reckoning, which looks past the amount to the heart and the cost. A great gift given easily out of abundance may be less in God’s sight than a small gift given at real sacrifice.

The principle to recover is the Lord’s own standard of giving: God weighs the heart and the sacrifice, not the sum. The widow gave two mites—a trifle by the world’s scale—yet the Lord said she gave more than all the rich, for they gave of their surplus and kept their security, but she gave her whole living and cast herself wholly upon God. The smallest gift given in love and faith, at genuine cost, is great in heaven; and the poorest saint who gives her all may give more than the wealthy, for she gives not merely her coins but herself. The widow’s mite is the abiding measure of acceptable giving.
roots_summary: The poor widow’s two coins, declared by the Lord more than all the rich gave; God weighs the gift by cost and love, not by the sum.

etymology: An enclosure for sheep; in Scripture, a figure of the people of God gathered and kept by the Shepherd; from the Old English scēap and fald.
biblical_def: The sheepfold is the enclosure where sheep are gathered and kept safe, and in the Lord’s great discourse of John 10 it becomes a figure of the people of God, with Christ Himself as both the door of the fold and the Good Shepherd of the sheep. He that enters not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber; but Christ is the door: by Him if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture. The sheep are His own, called by name; they hear His voice and follow Him, and a stranger they will not follow. And He looks beyond the one fold of Israel to gather the Gentiles too: other sheep I have, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd. The fold speaks of belonging, safety, and the watchful keeping of the Shepherd, who gives His life for the sheep and from whose hand none can pluck them. The dictionary reads the sheepfold as the figure of the church gathered and guarded by Christ: His own flock, entered only through Him the door, kept safe within His care, fed in His pasture, knowing His voice—Jew and Gentile gathered into one fold under one Shepherd, the people who are His and the sheep of His pasture.
webster_summary: The enclosure for sheep; a figure of the people of God gathered and kept by Christ, who is both the door of the fold and the Good Shepherd—one fold of Jew and Gentile under one Shepherd.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though men climb into the fold some other way than by Christ the door; Scripture knows one fold entered only through Him, kept safe under one Shepherd.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error the figure rebukes is the attempt to enter the fold some other way than by Christ the door. Every scheme of salvation that bypasses Christ—works, ritual, sincerity, another mediator, another way—is the climbing up of the thief and the robber, who comes not in by the door. There is one door into the fold of God’s people, and it is Christ; he that enters by Him is saved and finds pasture, but he that seeks another entrance is no true sheep but an intruder. The pluralism that imagines many doors into the one fold is answered by the Lord’s own claim: I am the door.

The principle to recover is the one fold of Christ, entered only through Him and kept under His care. The sheepfold is the people of God—His own flock, called by name, hearing His voice and following Him, entering by Him the door and finding safety and pasture within. And the fold is one: He gathers other sheep not of the fold of Israel, the Gentiles too, that there may be one fold and one shepherd. The figure speaks of belonging, of safety, and of the watchful keeping of the Shepherd who gave His life for the sheep and from whose hand none can pluck them. The church is His fold, and Christ alone its door and its keeper.
roots_summary: The enclosure for sheep; a figure of the people of God gathered and kept by Christ, the door of the fold and the Good Shepherd—one fold under one Shepherd.

etymology: The angels as servants of God sent to minister to the heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1:14); from the Latin ministrare, to serve.
biblical_def: Ministering spirits is the New Testament’s description of the holy angels in their service toward the people of God: Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation? The angels are created spirits, excelling in strength, who do God’s commandments, hearkening unto the voice of His word; and among their appointed works is the unseen service of the saints. God gives His angels charge over His own, to keep them in all their ways; the angel of the LORD encamps round about them that fear Him and delivers them. They rejoiced at the birth of Christ, strengthened Him in Gethsemane, rolled away the stone, and have carried the souls of the saints, as Lazarus was borne by angels into Abraham’s bosom. Yet their ministry is hidden and subordinate: they serve the heirs of salvation for Christ’s sake, and are never to be worshipped, for worship belongs to God alone, and even an angel forbade John to bow to him. The dictionary reads the ministering spirits as the holy angels in their loving, hidden service to the redeemed—sent forth by God to guard, strengthen, and aid the heirs of salvation—a comfort that the believer is never alone or unguarded, attended by unseen servants of his God; with the caution that the angels point always to Christ, are never to be worshipped or invoked, and minister not to themselves but to the heirs of the great salvation.
webster_summary: The holy angels as God’s servants, sent forth to minister to the heirs of salvation; a hidden, loving service—a comfort that the believer is guarded, with the caution that angels are never to be worshipped.

corruption_summary: Angels are either dismissed as myth or wrongly venerated and invoked; Scripture knows them as God’s servants ministering to the saints, never to be worshipped, pointing always to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite errors touch the ministering spirits. The first is the modern dismissal of angels as myth or sentiment—the reduction of God’s mighty servants to nursery decoration or the denial of them altogether by a materialism that allows no unseen world. The second, opposite error is the veneration and invocation of angels, the cult of guardian angels and the praying to them, which Scripture forbids—for worship belongs to God alone, and the angel in the Revelation refused John’s worship, saying, see thou do it not; worship God. The angels are neither to be denied nor adored.

The principle to recover is the angels as God’s servants ministering to the saints for Christ’s sake. They are ministering spirits, sent forth to minister to the heirs of salvation—mighty, holy creatures who do God’s commandments and are charged to keep His people in all their ways, guarding, strengthening, and aiding the redeemed in service unseen. This is a great comfort: the believer is never alone or unguarded, attended by the servants of his God. Yet their ministry is hidden and subordinate; they point always to Christ, are never to be worshipped or invoked, and serve not themselves but the heirs of the great salvation, to the glory of the God who sends them.

etymology: An angelic being who watches and executes God’s decree (Daniel 4:13, 17); from the wakeful, watching character of the heavenly host.
biblical_def: A watcher is an angelic being named in the visions of Daniel—a watcher and an holy one came down from heaven—who watches over the affairs of men and executes the decrees of the Most High. In Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, the felling of the great tree is pronounced by the decree of the watchers, the demand by the word of the holy ones, to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. The watchers are thus the wakeful servants of God’s providence, attending His throne, observing the doings of men, and carrying out His sentences upon kings and nations. Their name fittingly expresses a truth of the whole heavenly host and of God Himself: the eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good; He that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. Nothing escapes the wakeful watch of heaven; the proud king is humbled by the decree of the watchers, that he may learn who truly reigns. The dictionary reads the watcher as the figure of God’s sleepless oversight of the world—the angelic watcher executing the divine decree, and behind him the unsleeping God whose eyes run to and fro throughout the whole earth—a solemn warning to the proud that heaven watches and judges, and a comfort to the saint that the God who keeps him never slumbers nor sleeps.
webster_summary: An angelic being of Daniel’s visions who watches over men and executes God’s decree; a figure of heaven’s sleepless oversight—warning to the proud, comfort to the saint whose Keeper never sleeps.

corruption_summary: Apocryphal and occult traditions spin the “watchers” into elaborate myths of fallen angelic origins; Scripture names them holy servants of God’s decree, figures of heaven’s sleepless oversight.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the spinning of the “watchers” into elaborate myth. Apocryphal works such as 1 Enoch, and the occult and speculative traditions that feed on them, build whole mythologies of fallen “Watchers” who corrupted mankind—legends that have gripped imaginations but rest on no canonical foundation. The dictionary keeps to Scripture. In Daniel the watcher is a holy one, an angelic servant of the Most High who comes down from heaven to pronounce and execute God’s decree; he is no rogue or fallen being but an instrument of divine providence. The canon, not the apocrypha, governs what we believe of the watchers.

The principle to recover is the sleepless oversight of God over the world. The watcher of Daniel executes the decree of the Most High, that the living may know that He rules in the kingdom of men and sets up whom He will—humbling the proud Nebuchadnezzar until he learns who truly reigns. And the watcher’s name expresses a truth of God Himself: His eyes are in every place, beholding the evil and the good, and He that keeps His people neither slumbers nor sleeps. Heaven watches; nothing escapes its eye. This is a solemn warning to the proud, who imagine no one sees, and a deep comfort to the saint, whose Keeper is awake and watching over him through every night.
roots_summary: An angelic being of Daniel’s visions who watches and executes God’s decree; a figure of heaven’s sleepless oversight—warning to the proud, comfort to the saint.
